title: Honey never spoils.
explain: Sealed jars found in 3,000-year-old Egyptian tombs were still perfectly edible — its low moisture and acidity keep bacteria from surviving.

title: A shuffled deck is one of a kind.
explain: Fifty-two cards can be arranged in 52 factorial ways — a number vastly larger than the atoms estimated on Earth.

title: Water can be boiling and freezing at once.
explain: At its exact 'triple point' — one specific temperature and pressure — water exists as solid ice, liquid, and vapor all at the same time.

title: A metal exists that melts in your hand.
explain: Gallium has a melting point of about 29.8°C, just above body temperature, so a solid gallium spoon starts turning liquid the moment you hold it.

title: Hot water can freeze faster than cold water.
explain: Known as the Mpemba effect, it's been observed for centuries under the right conditions — and scientists still don't fully agree on why it happens.

title: Diamonds may rain from the sky — on other planets.
explain: Scientists believe the extreme pressure inside Neptune and Uranus can crush carbon into diamonds, which then sink slowly through the planets' interiors.

title: A neutron star is unimaginably dense.
explain: A sugar-cube-sized piece would weigh about as much as a small mountain — the result of a collapsed star crushed under its own gravity.

title: Sound can't travel through space.
explain: Space is a near-total vacuum, and sound needs molecules to vibrate through — without air, dust, or gas nearby, there's nothing for it to move across.

title: Bananas are slightly radioactive.
explain: They contain potassium-40, a naturally radioactive isotope. The dose is tiny: you'd need to eat millions at once for it to matter.

title: Helium doesn't actually raise your voice's pitch.
explain: Your vocal cords vibrate the same. Sound travels faster through helium, which shifts the resonance of your throat and makes you sound squeaky.

title: Atoms are almost entirely empty space.
explain: If an atom were the size of a stadium, its nucleus would be about the size of a pea sitting in the middle.

title: Water expands when it freezes.
explain: Unlike most substances, water gets less dense as a solid. That's why ice floats and lakes freeze from the top down, protecting life below.

title: Earth's core is about as hot as the sun's surface.
explain: The inner core is estimated at roughly 5,200°C, close to the sun's surface temperature of about 5,500°C.

title: You are partly made of stardust.
explain: Many elements in your body, like the calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood, were forged inside stars that exploded long ago.

title: The microwave oven was invented by accident.
explain: In 1945, engineer Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket while working near radar equipment, and followed the clue.

title: Penicillin was discovered on a forgotten dish.
explain: In 1928, Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find mold had killed the bacteria in a petri dish he'd left out.

title: Octopuses have three hearts.
explain: Two pump blood to the gills, one to the rest of the body — and that third heart stops beating when the octopus swims.

title: Wombats poop in cubes.
explain: The unusual shape keeps the droppings from rolling away once stacked up to mark territory.

title: Sharks are older than trees.
explain: Sharks have existed for over 400 million years — roughly 50 million years before the first trees appeared.

title: Sea otters hold hands while they sleep.
explain: They link paws in groups called 'rafts' so the ocean current doesn't drift them apart while they doze.

title: Tardigrades can survive the vacuum of space.
explain: These microscopic animals have been exposed directly to open space and radiation in orbit and revived afterward, unharmed.

title: Flamingos are born gray, not pink.
explain: Their signature color comes from pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat — without that diet, they'd stay a dull gray-white.

title: Bees can recognize individual human faces.
explain: Despite having a brain smaller than a grain of rice, honeybees can learn to tell different human faces apart in photos.

title: Elephants are the only mammal that can't jump.
explain: Their sheer weight and leg-bone structure mean all four feet can never leave the ground at once, unlike almost every other mammal.

title: A snail can sleep for up to three years.
explain: When conditions turn too hot, cold, or dry, snails seal themselves into their shells and enter a dormant state to wait it out.

title: Cows form close friendships.
explain: Studies have found cows kept with a preferred companion show measurably lower stress levels than when separated from them.

title: A blue whale's heart can weigh 180 kg.
explain: It's the largest heart of any animal on Earth, and its beat can be detected from kilometers away underwater.

title: Koalas have fingerprints almost like ours.
explain: They're so similar to human prints that even under a microscope they can be hard to tell apart.

title: Hummingbirds can fly backwards.
explain: Their wings rotate in a figure-eight motion, letting them hover, fly in reverse, and even briefly fly upside down.

title: Axolotls can regrow entire limbs.
explain: These salamanders can regenerate legs, parts of their heart, and even sections of their brain without scarring.

title: Crows remember human faces for years.
explain: Researchers found crows recognized people who'd threatened them, scolded them on sight, and taught other crows to do the same.

title: Giraffes have the same number of neck bones as you.
explain: Both have seven neck vertebrae. A giraffe's are just much longer, each up to about 25 cm.

title: Starfish have no blood.
explain: Instead of blood, they pump filtered seawater through their bodies to carry nutrients around.

title: Owls can't move their eyes.
explain: Their eyes are fixed in their sockets, so owls rotate their heads up to about 270 degrees to look around.

title: A shrimp's snap can briefly be hotter than the sun's surface.
explain: The pistol shrimp snaps its claw so fast it creates a collapsing bubble that reaches thousands of degrees for an instant.

title: Dolphins sleep with half their brain at a time.
explain: One half rests while the other stays alert, letting them keep breathing and watch for danger.

title: Lightning is hotter than the surface of the sun.
explain: A single bolt reaches roughly 30,000 Kelvin — about five times hotter than the sun's surface temperature.

title: Venus is the only planet that spins clockwise.
explain: Every other planet in the solar system rotates counter-clockwise, seen from above the sun's north pole.

title: A day on Venus is longer than its year.
explain: Venus takes 243 Earth days to rotate once, but only 225 Earth days to orbit the sun.

title: There are more stars than grains of sand on Earth.
explain: Astronomers estimate roughly a septillion stars in the observable universe — far more than the sand on every beach and desert combined.

title: Some dead stars spin 600 times a second.
explain: The fastest known pulsars — collapsed cores of exploded stars — rotate several hundred times per second, fast enough to blur past comprehension.

title: Saturn would float in water.
explain: It's the only planet in the solar system less dense than water — with a bathtub big enough, the whole planet would float.

title: The footprints on the Moon will last millions of years.
explain: With no wind, water, or atmosphere to erode them, the boot prints left by Apollo astronauts are expected to stay visible for millions of years.

title: Over a million Earths could fit inside the sun.
explain: The sun's diameter is about 109 times that of Earth, giving it enough volume to contain roughly 1.3 million Earth-sized planets.

title: A year on Mercury is just 88 Earth days.
explain: Mercury's tight, fast orbit around the sun means it completes a full year in less time than it takes Earth to finish three months.

title: Uranus rotates on its side.
explain: Its axis is tilted about 98 degrees, likely from an ancient collision — so unlike every other planet, it essentially rolls around the sun.

title: Astronauts on the ISS see about 16 sunrises a day.
explain: The station orbits Earth roughly every 90 minutes, passing from day to night and back again 16 times in 24 hours.

title: Mars has a volcano nearly 3 times taller than Everest.
explain: Olympus Mons rises about 22 km high and is roughly as wide as France.

title: Jupiter has a storm bigger than Earth.
explain: The Great Red Spot is wider than our planet and has been raging for at least 150 years, possibly much longer.

title: The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth.
explain: It moves about 3.8 cm farther away each year, roughly the rate your fingernails grow.

title: Sunlight is about 8 minutes old when it reaches you.
explain: Light takes roughly 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel the 150 million km from the sun to Earth.

title: Sunsets on Mars are blue.
explain: Fine Martian dust scatters light differently than Earth's air, giving the sky around the setting sun a blue glow.

title: Astronauts grow taller in space.
explain: Without gravity compressing the spine, astronauts can gain up to about 3% in height, which shrinks back on return.

title: Our galaxy is on a collision course.
explain: The Milky Way and Andromeda are expected to merge in around 4 to 5 billion years.

title: Neptune completed its first orbit since discovery in 2011.
explain: A year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years, and it was only discovered in 1846.

title: Astronauts say space smells like seared steak.
explain: After spacewalks, astronauts report a metallic, burnt smell clinging to their suits, often compared to hot metal or grilled meat.

title: The shortest war on record lasted 38 minutes.
explain: Britain defeated Zanzibar on 27 August 1896, in what's recognised as history's briefest declared war.

title: The Great Wall of China isn't visible from space.
explain: Despite the popular myth, astronauts have confirmed it's not distinguishable with the naked eye from orbit.

title: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids.
explain: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC; Cleopatra ruled around 30 BC — closer in time to Apollo 11 in 1969 than to the pyramid's construction.

title: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire.
explain: Teaching at Oxford began around 1096, while the Aztec civilization wasn't founded until 1325 — over two centuries later.

title: Woolly mammoths were still alive when the pyramids were built.
explain: A small population survived on Wrangel Island until about 1650 BC, overlapping with the early dynasties of ancient Egypt.

title: France used the guillotine the same year Star Wars came out.
explain: France's last execution by guillotine took place in 1977 — the same year the original 'Star Wars' premiered in theaters.

title: The first known recipe is nearly 4,000 years old.
explain: Clay tablets from ancient Mesopotamia, dated to around 1730 BC, record cooking instructions for stews — the oldest written recipes known.

title: Napoleon was once attacked by a horde of rabbits.
explain: During a staged hunting event in 1807, thousands of released rabbits swarmed his party instead of fleeing, forcing a retreat to his carriage.

title: The Eiffel Tower was almost torn down after 20 years.
explain: It was built in 1889 as a temporary exhibit with a 20-year permit, and was saved from demolition only because it proved useful for radio transmission.

title: Vikings never actually wore horned helmets.
explain: No genuine Viking-era helmet with horns has ever been found — the image comes from 19th-century opera costumes, centuries after the Viking age ended.

title: Ancient Romans whitened their teeth with urine.
explain: The ammonia in urine acts as a cleaning agent, and Roman writers mention it being used as a mouthwash.

title: The oldest recorded joke is about a fart.
explain: A Sumerian joke from around 1900 BC is widely cited as the oldest one on record, and it's toilet humor.

title: Tug of war used to be an Olympic sport.
explain: It was part of the Summer Olympics from 1900 to 1920, with teams from several countries competing for medals.

title: Anne Frank and Martin Luther King Jr. were born the same year.
explain: Both were born in 1929, which shows how recent these seemingly distant chapters of history are.

title: Nintendo was founded in 1889.
explain: Long before video games, it started as a company making hand-made playing cards in Kyoto.

title: The pyramids were likely built by paid workers.
explain: Tombs of laborers found near Giza suggest the builders were skilled, fed, and honored, not slaves as long believed.

title: Abraham Lincoln is in the Wrestling Hall of Fame.
explain: He wrestled as a young man and reportedly lost only one of around 300 matches, earning an honorary induction.

title: The fax machine was invented before the telephone.
explain: Alexander Bain patented an early fax device in 1843, over 30 years before the telephone was patented in 1876.

title: Queen Elizabeth II trained as a mechanic.
explain: During World War II, she joined the women's auxiliary army and learned to drive and repair military vehicles.

title: Coffee was once banned in Mecca.
explain: In 1511, authorities outlawed coffee because coffeehouses were seen as hotbeds of dissent. The ban didn't last.

title: Bananas are berries. Strawberries aren't.
explain: Botanically, a berry develops from one ovary with seeds inside the flesh — bananas qualify, strawberries don't.

title: Carrots were originally purple, not orange.
explain: The now-familiar orange carrot was bred in the Netherlands around the 17th century; earlier carrots were typically purple, white, or yellow.

title: Chocolate was once used as currency.
explain: The Aztecs and Maya valued cacao beans highly enough to use them as money, sometimes trading a single bean for a small tamale.

title: Peanuts aren't actually nuts.
explain: They're legumes that grow underground, more closely related to beans and lentils than to tree nuts like almonds or walnuts.

title: White chocolate isn't technically chocolate.
explain: It contains cocoa butter but no cocoa solids — the part that gives chocolate its color and much of its flavor — so many definitions exclude it.

title: Apples float because they're 25% air.
explain: Roughly a quarter of an apple's volume is air pockets between its cells, which is enough to make it less dense than water.

title: Ketchup was sold as medicine in the 1830s.
explain: A doctor marketed tomato-based ketchup pills as a cure for indigestion and other ailments before it became a condiment.

title: Almonds are technically a seed, not a nut.
explain: An almond is the seed found inside the pit of a fruit closely related to peaches and plums — botanically closer to a stone fruit seed than a true nut.

title: Most restaurant wasabi isn't real wasabi.
explain: Genuine wasabi root is rare and expensive, so most sushi restaurants outside Japan serve dyed horseradish and mustard instead.

title: Vanilla is the second most expensive spice in the world.
explain: Because the vanilla orchid must be hand-pollinated and each pod cured for months, real vanilla is extraordinarily labor-intensive to produce.

title: A pineapple takes about two years to grow.
explain: Each plant typically produces just one pineapple at a time, after around 18 to 24 months.

title: Cashews grow outside a fruit.
explain: Each nut hangs from the bottom of a 'cashew apple', and its shell contains an irritating oil related to poison ivy.

title: Sliced bread wasn't sold until 1928.
explain: It was first sold pre-sliced in Chillicothe, Missouri, which is where the phrase 'the best thing since sliced bread' comes from.

title: Coca-Cola once contained cocaine.
explain: Early versions used coca leaf extract, and the cocaine was removed from the recipe in the early 1900s.

title: Many figs are pollinated by wasps.
explain: Tiny female wasps crawl inside to lay eggs and often die there. The fig breaks them down, so you don't eat a whole wasp.

title: The potato was the first vegetable grown in space.
explain: In 1995, potato plants were grown aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia as part of an experiment.

title: The popsicle was invented by an 11-year-old.
explain: In 1905, Frank Epperson left a cup of soda with a stirring stick outside overnight. It froze, and he later patented the idea.

title: Birds can't feel the heat of chili peppers.
explain: They lack the receptor that reacts to capsaicin, which helps them spread chili seeds that mammals would avoid.

title: Europeans once feared tomatoes were poisonous.
explain: The tomato belongs to the nightshade family, and many Europeans viewed it with suspicion for centuries.

title: Worcestershire sauce is made with fermented fish.
explain: Anchovies are a key ingredient, fermented for months to give the sauce its deep, savory flavor.

title: Scotland's national animal is the unicorn.
explain: It's appeared on Scottish royal symbols since the 1300s, chosen for its associations with purity and strength.

title: Finland has more saunas than cars.
explain: With roughly 2 million saunas for a population of about 5.5 million, saunas are deeply embedded in daily Finnish life.

title: Denmark has a word for cozy contentment.
explain: 'Hygge' describes a feeling of warm, comfortable togetherness — there's no direct English translation, and the concept has become a lifestyle export.

title: Japan has more vending machines per person than anywhere else.
explain: There's roughly one vending machine for every 23 people in Japan, selling everything from hot coffee to fresh eggs and umbrellas.

title: Bhutan measures progress using happiness, not just GDP.
explain: Since the 1970s, Bhutan has used a 'Gross National Happiness' index alongside economic measures to guide national policy.

title: The shortest place name in the world is one letter.
explain: Several villages — including ones in Norway and Sweden — are officially named just 'Å,' a single Scandinavian letter.

title: The handshake may have started as a weapons check.
explain: One popular historical theory holds that gripping and shaking an open right hand showed you weren't concealing a weapon.

title: The depth of a bow changes its meaning in Japan.
explain: A quick nod signals something very different from a deep, held bow — the angle and duration communicate the level of respect or apology intended.

title: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world.
explain: At about 0.44 square kilometers, it's smaller than most golf courses, with a resident population of only a few hundred people.

title: Iceland has no mosquitoes.
explain: It's one of the only inhabited places on Earth where the insect can't establish itself, thanks to its particular climate and volcanic soil chemistry.

title: Norway's army has a knighted penguin.
explain: Sir Nils Olav, a king penguin at Edinburgh Zoo, holds an honorary rank in the Norwegian King's Guard.

title: Finland hosts a wife-carrying championship.
explain: Competitors race through an obstacle course carrying a partner, and the prize has traditionally included the partner's weight in beer.

title: Hawaiian pizza was invented in Canada.
explain: Greek-Canadian restaurant owner Sam Panopoulos first put pineapple on pizza in Ontario in 1962.

title: South Koreans used to be one year old at birth.
explain: The traditional counting age added a year at birth and every New Year, until the country officially switched in 2023.

title: Denmark has the oldest national flag still in use.
explain: The red and white Dannebrog dates back centuries, with legend placing its origin in 1219.

title: Nepal's flag is the only non-rectangular national flag.
explain: It's made of two stacked triangles, representing the Himalayas and two major religions.

title: In Switzerland, you can't own just one guinea pig.
explain: Animal welfare law requires social animals like guinea pigs to be kept with at least one companion.

title: Iceland has a committee that approves baby names.
explain: New names must fit Icelandic grammar and spelling, or parents need approval from the official naming committee.

title: Ireland's national symbol is the harp, not the shamrock.
explain: The harp appears on Irish coins, passports, and the presidential seal, and is the official state emblem.

title: The Netherlands has more bikes than people.
explain: There are an estimated 23 million bicycles for a population of about 18 million.

title: The human body gives off a faint glow.
explain: Chemical reactions inside your cells produce a small amount of visible light, far too dim to see, but detectable with sensitive enough cameras.

title: Your stomach relines itself every few days.
explain: Stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve metal over time, so your stomach replaces its protective mucus lining roughly every 3 to 5 days to avoid digesting itself.

title: The DNA in one cell stretches about 2 meters.
explain: It's packed into a nucleus far too small to see, coiled tightly around proteins so the whole strand fits.

title: Your brain uses about 20% of your body's energy.
explain: It makes up only around 2% of your body weight, yet it burns roughly a fifth of the calories you use at rest.

title: Old windows aren't thicker at the bottom because glass flows.
explain: Glass is a solid. Old panes are uneven because of how they were made, and glaziers often put the thick edge at the bottom.

title: Diamonds and pencil lead are the same element.
explain: Both are pure carbon. The only difference is how the atoms are arranged.

title: Sound travels about four times faster in water.
explain: Around 1,480 m/s in water versus about 343 m/s in air, because water molecules are packed closer together.

title: Liquid oxygen is pale blue and magnetic.
explain: Pour it between the poles of a strong magnet and it sticks there.

title: A fluffy cloud can weigh around 500 tonnes.
explain: A typical cumulus cloud holds that much water, spread as tiny droplets over a huge volume of air.

title: Light slows down in glass.
explain: In glass, light travels at roughly two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum. That slowdown is what makes lenses bend it.

title: Mirrors don't flip left and right.
explain: They flip front to back. Your left hand stays on the left side of the mirror; it's depth that gets reversed.

title: The Eiffel Tower grows in summer.
explain: Heat makes its iron expand, so the tower can be about 15 cm taller on a hot day.

title: You can never quite reach absolute zero.
explain: At −273.15°C, particles would have the least possible energy. Labs get within billionths of a degree, but never all the way.

title: The coldest known places in the universe are in labs.
explain: Physicists cool atoms to billionths of a degree above absolute zero, far colder than anywhere in deep space.

title: Popcorn pops because of steam.
explain: Water inside the kernel turns to steam, pressure builds until the hull bursts, and the starch puffs out.

title: Snow is actually clear.
explain: Each ice crystal is transparent. Snow looks white because its many surfaces scatter all colors of light.

title: A rubber band heats up when you stretch it.
explain: Stretching lines up its long molecules and releases heat. Let it relax and it cools down. You can feel it against your lip.

title: Some metals burst into flame in water.
explain: Sodium and potassium react so violently with water that the hydrogen they release can ignite.

title: Sand can scratch your phone screen.
explain: Most sand is quartz, which is harder than the glass on many phones. That's where a lot of scratches come from.

title: Trees are mostly made of air.
explain: Most of a tree's mass comes from carbon dioxide pulled out of the air, not from the soil.

title: Pure water barely conducts electricity.
explain: It's the dissolved salts and minerals in everyday water that let current flow.

title: The smell of rain has a name: petrichor.
explain: Much of it comes from geosmin, made by soil bacteria. Human noses can detect it at a few parts per trillion.

title: Chalk is made of tiny fossils.
explain: Natural chalk is built from the shells of microscopic ocean algae that piled up on ancient seafloors.

title: Einstein's Nobel Prize wasn't for relativity.
explain: He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for explaining the photoelectric effect.

title: Atomic clocks barely ever drift.
explain: The best cesium clocks would lose about one second in 100 million years, and newer optical clocks are even better.

title: Superfluid helium can climb walls.
explain: Cooled close to absolute zero, liquid helium loses all friction and creeps up and over the sides of its container.

title: Your microwave and your Wi-Fi share a frequency.
explain: Both commonly use around 2.4 GHz, which is why an old microwave can make Wi-Fi drop out.

title: There are 118 confirmed elements.
explain: The last four were officially named in 2016: nihonium, moscovium, tennessine and oganesson.

title: Aerogel is about 99.8% air.
explain: It's one of the lightest solids ever made and an extremely good insulator.

title: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance.
explain: Fitting for a bird that stands out that much.

title: One jellyfish can age in reverse.
explain: Turritopsis dohrnii can turn back into its juvenile polyp stage when stressed, starting its life cycle again.

title: Pigeons can tell Picasso from Monet.
explain: In a 1995 study, trained pigeons learned to tell paintings by the two artists apart.

title: Male seahorses give birth.
explain: The female puts her eggs into the male's pouch, and he carries them until they hatch.

title: Zebra stripes may keep flies away.
explain: Studies found biting flies struggle to land on striped surfaces, which may be why zebras have them.

title: Polar bears have black skin.
explain: Their fur isn't white either: each hair is translucent and scatters light, which makes it look white.

title: Dolphins have names.
explain: Each dolphin develops a signature whistle, and others use it to call that specific individual.

title: Sloths can hold their breath for 40 minutes.
explain: They can slow their heart rate way down, which helps them stay underwater far longer than most mammals.

title: Honeybees dance to give directions.
explain: The waggle dance tells other bees the direction and distance to a food source.

title: Mantis shrimp can break aquarium glass.
explain: Their club-like arms strike with the acceleration of a bullet, fast enough to boil the water around them.

title: Platypuses glow under UV light.
explain: Their fur fluoresces blue-green. Males also have venomous spurs on their back legs.

title: Rats laugh when tickled.
explain: They make ultrasonic chirps too high for us to hear, and they come back for more.

title: Ants don't have lungs.
explain: Air enters through tiny holes along their bodies called spiracles and moves through a network of tubes.

title: Arctic terns fly the longest migration of any animal.
explain: They travel from the Arctic to Antarctica and back each year, often more than 70,000 km.

title: Butterflies taste with their feet.
explain: Sensors on their feet tell them whether a leaf is the right plant to lay eggs on.

title: Goats have rectangular pupils.
explain: The wide shape gives them a panoramic view to spot predators while grazing.

title: A day on Mercury lasts two of its years.
explain: From sunrise to sunrise takes 176 Earth days, while one orbit around the Sun takes 88.

title: There's a water cloud in space bigger than all Earth's oceans.
explain: Around a distant quasar, astronomers found water vapor equal to about 140 trillion times Earth's oceans.

title: The Sun holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass.
explain: All the planets, moons, asteroids and comets together make up the tiny remainder.

title: Pluto hasn't finished one orbit since it was discovered.
explain: It was found in 1930, and one trip around the Sun takes about 248 years.

title: Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object.
explain: Launched in 1977, it's now more than 24 billion km away and still sending signals.

title: Venus is hotter than Mercury.
explain: Even though it's farther from the Sun, its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat at about 465°C.

title: Mars has a canyon as long as the United States is wide.
explain: Valles Marineris stretches about 4,000 km and is up to 7 km deep.

title: The Moon has earthquakes.
explain: Moonquakes happen, and some last much longer than earthquakes because the Moon is so dry and rigid.

title: There's no 'dark side' of the Moon.
explain: The far side gets just as much sunlight. We just never see it from Earth, because the Moon always shows us the same face.

title: Some 'stars' are colder than the North Pole.
explain: Brown dwarfs are failed stars, and the coldest known one is below freezing.

title: Space starts about 100 km up.
explain: That's the Kármán line, roughly an hour's drive away if you could drive straight up.

title: One of Mars's moons is doomed.
explain: Phobos is slowly spiraling inward and will likely break apart or crash into Mars in about 50 million years.

title: The Voyager probes carry a golden record.
explain: It holds sounds, music and images from Earth, just in case anyone ever finds it.

title: Napoleon wasn't actually short.
explain: He was about 1.69 m, average for a Frenchman of his time. Confusion between French and English inches helped the myth.

title: The Great Fire of London had few recorded deaths.
explain: The 1666 fire destroyed much of the city, but only six deaths were officially recorded. The real number was likely higher.

title: Ancient Romans used urine to wash clothes.
explain: Its ammonia helped clean fabric, and urine was collected from public pots for laundries.

title: Einstein was offered the presidency of Israel.
explain: In 1952 he was asked to become president. He politely declined.

title: The first known author was a woman.
explain: Enheduanna, a Mesopotamian priestess around 2300 BC, is the earliest author known by name.

title: Ten days vanished in 1582.
explain: To fix the calendar, the Gregorian switch jumped straight from October 4 to October 15 in several countries.

title: Russia's October Revolution happened in November.
explain: Russia still used the old Julian calendar in 1917. By today's calendar, the revolution was in November.

title: The Colosseum may have hosted mock sea battles.
explain: Ancient writers describe it being flooded for naval shows in its early years.

title: Harvard is older than calculus.
explain: Harvard was founded in 1636. Newton and Leibniz developed calculus decades later.

title: Ancient Egyptians slept on stone headrests.
explain: Instead of soft pillows, many used curved headrests made of wood or stone.

title: The first recorded Olympic champion was a cook.
explain: Coroebus of Elis won the footrace in 776 BC.

title: Roman concrete gets stronger in seawater.
explain: Harbor walls built 2,000 years ago are still standing because seawater helps grow new minerals inside them.

title: China used paper money a thousand years ago.
explain: Paper currency spread in China during the Song dynasty, centuries before Europe.

title: Australia lost a war against emus.
explain: In 1932, soldiers with machine guns failed to cull the emus damaging crops in Western Australia.

title: The chess queen used to be one of the weakest pieces.
explain: It could only move one square diagonally until a rule change in 15th-century Europe made it the strongest.

title: Einstein's brain was taken after he died.
explain: The pathologist who did the autopsy in 1955 kept it, without clear permission, for decades.

title: The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years.
explain: It ran from 1337 to 1453, with long breaks in between.

title: Ancient Romans had fast food.
explain: Street counters called thermopolia sold hot food and drinks, and some have been found in Pompeii.

title: A 1904 Olympic marathon runner rode in a car.
explain: Fred Lorz hitched a ride for part of the course and crossed the line first before being caught.

title: The lighter was invented before the match.
explain: Döbereiner's lamp, an early lighter, dates from 1823. Friction matches came a few years later.

title: The Statue of Liberty used to be copper-colored.
explain: It was shiny brown copper at first and turned green over about 30 years as the metal oxidized.

title: Pistachios can catch fire on their own.
explain: Stored in large piles, they can heat up and spontaneously combust, so shipping rules cover them.

title: Sliced bread was banned in the US.
explain: In 1943, the government briefly banned it to save resources during the war. It lasted about two months.

title: Ripe cranberries bounce.
explain: Growers have used bounce tests to sort good cranberries from bad ones.

title: Fortune cookies aren't from China.
explain: They trace back to Japan and were popularized in California in the early 1900s.

title: Caesar salad was invented in Mexico.
explain: Restaurateur Caesar Cardini is credited with creating it in Tijuana in the 1920s.

title: Broccoli, kale and cabbage are the same species.
explain: They, along with cauliflower and Brussels sprouts, were all bred from one wild mustard plant.

title: Coffee beans are seeds from a fruit.
explain: They grow inside a red fruit called a coffee cherry.

title: Avocados are berries.
explain: Botanically, an avocado is a large berry with a single seed.

title: Croissants have Austrian roots.
explain: They grew out of the Austrian kipferl, adapted by bakers in Paris.

title: Rice feeds more than half the world.
explain: It's a staple food for more than half of the global population.

title: The holes in Swiss cheese come from bacteria.
explain: Bacteria release carbon dioxide bubbles as the cheese ages, and tiny hay particles help the holes form.

title: Green bell peppers are unripe.
explain: Left on the plant, most green peppers turn yellow, orange or red and get sweeter.

title: Nachos are named after a man called Nacho.
explain: Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya created them in Mexico in 1943 for some visiting guests.

title: Traditional Parmesan isn't vegetarian.
explain: Parmigiano Reggiano is made with animal rennet from calves.

title: Kiwifruit was renamed for marketing.
explain: It used to be called the Chinese gooseberry. New Zealand exporters renamed it after their national bird.

title: Canned food came before the can opener.
explain: Early cans were opened with hammers and chisels for decades before a proper opener was invented.

title: KFC is a Christmas tradition in Japan.
explain: Thanks to a 1970s ad campaign, millions of Japanese families order fried chicken for Christmas.

title: The Mona Lisa has no eyebrows.
explain: They may have faded over time or been removed by cleaning. High-res scans suggest there were once faint ones.

title: The Mona Lisa became famous after it was stolen.
explain: Its theft from the Louvre in 1911 made headlines worldwide and turned it into a global icon.

title: Van Gogh sold very few paintings while alive.
explain: He's known to have sold very little, and he died with almost no commercial success.

title: Monopoly was meant as a warning.
explain: It began as The Landlord's Game, designed by Lizzie Magie to show the problems with land monopolies.

title: Iceland celebrates Christmas with a book flood.
explain: Called Jólabókaflóð, it's a tradition of giving books on Christmas Eve and reading them that night.

title: Norway gives London a Christmas tree every year.
explain: Since 1947, Oslo has sent a tree to Trafalgar Square to thank Britain for its help in World War II.

title: 'Happy Birthday' was under copyright until 2016.
explain: A court ruling ended the claim, and the song is now in the public domain.

title: Scrabble's letter values came from a newspaper.
explain: Its inventor counted letter frequency on New York Times front pages to set the points.

title: A Rubik's Cube has 43 quintillion combinations.
explain: Yet any position can be solved in 20 moves or fewer.

title: Barbie has a full name.
explain: She's Barbara Millicent Roberts, from the fictional town of Willows, Wisconsin.

title: Lego makes more tires than any tire company.
explain: By count, it produces hundreds of millions of tiny tires every year.

title: Tetris was created in the Soviet Union.
explain: Alexey Pajitnov developed it in 1984 at a computer center in Moscow.

title: The oldest known instruments are about 40,000 years old.
explain: Flutes made from bird bone and mammoth ivory have been found in caves in Germany.

title: The Hollywood sign used to say 'Hollywoodland'.
explain: It was an ad for a housing development in 1923. The 'land' was removed in 1949.

title: Every flag has at least one Olympic ring color.
explain: The designer chose blue, yellow, black, green and red on white so every nation's flag was represented.

title: Japan has more pets than children.
explain: There are more pet cats and dogs in Japan than children under 15.

title: The Phantom of the Opera is Broadway's longest-running show.
explain: It ran for 35 years before closing in 2023.

title: Sherlock Holmes never says 'Elementary, my dear Watson' in the books.
explain: The famous line comes from later films and adaptations.

title: Nobody says 'Play it again, Sam' in Casablanca.
explain: The actual line is closer to 'Play it, Sam.'

title: A Spanish town holds a giant tomato fight.
explain: Every August, thousands throw tomatoes at each other during La Tomatina in Buñol.

title: Russian nesting dolls are only about 130 years old.
explain: The first set was made in the 1890s, inspired by a Japanese doll.

title: One company lasted over 1,400 years.
explain: Kongō Gumi, a Japanese temple builder, was founded in 578 and ran independently until 2006.

title: Nigeria makes more films than Hollywood.
explain: Nollywood produces more movies per year than the US film industry, second only to India.

title: You're taller in the morning.
explain: The discs in your spine compress during the day, so you can be about 1 cm shorter by evening.

title: Your nose may detect a trillion smells.
explain: A 2014 study estimated humans can tell apart over a trillion scents, though scientists still debate the number.

title: Babies have more bones than adults.
explain: Newborns have around 300 bones, and many fuse together until adults have 206.

title: Your smallest bone is in your ear.
explain: The stapes is about 3 mm long and helps carry sound to your inner ear.

title: Bone handles more pressure than concrete.
explain: It can withstand higher compression than regular concrete while staying much lighter.

title: Your eyes see the world upside down.
explain: The lens flips the image on your retina, and your brain turns it right side up.

title: Your blood vessels could wrap around Earth twice.
explain: Laid end to end, an adult's vessels are estimated at around 100,000 km.

title: You can't tickle yourself.
explain: Your brain predicts the sensation of your own movements and dulls the response.

title: Fingernails grow faster than toenails.
explain: Fingernails grow about 3 mm a month, roughly three times faster than toenails.

title: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
explain: That's around 35 million beats a year.

title: Goosebumps are left over from our furry ancestors.
explain: The muscles that make your hairs stand up once fluffed out fur for warmth or to look bigger.

title: You shed tens of thousands of skin cells every minute.
explain: Your outer layer of skin is replaced continuously, roughly every month.

title: Tooth enamel is the hardest thing in your body.
explain: It's even harder than bone, but it can't repair itself.

title: Your taste buds are replaced every week or two.
explain: Taste receptor cells live around 10 days before new ones take over.

title: Your lungs aren't the same size.
explain: The left lung is smaller to make room for your heart, with two lobes instead of three.

title: You don't sneeze in your sleep.
explain: The reflex is suppressed while you sleep. A strong enough irritant wakes you up first.

title: Your corneas have no blood vessels.
explain: They get oxygen directly from the air instead.

title: Muscles can only pull.
explain: They never push, which is why they work in pairs, like biceps and triceps.

title: Your liver can grow back.
explain: It can regenerate to full size even after a large part of it is removed.

title: Your red blood cells have no nucleus.
explain: They lose it as they mature, making more room for oxygen-carrying hemoglobin.

title: You make about 2 million red blood cells every second.
explain: Your bone marrow keeps up with cells that wear out after around 120 days.

title: You have about as many hair follicles as a chimpanzee.
explain: Most of your hairs are just very fine and short.

title: Your small intestine is about 6 meters long.
explain: It's folded up to fit inside your abdomen.

title: Identical twins have different fingerprints.
explain: Fingerprints form in the womb and are shaped by tiny differences in position and pressure.

title: Your gut has its own nervous system.
explain: The enteric nervous system has hundreds of millions of neurons and can work largely on its own.

title: Your ears get longer as you age.
explain: Studies show ears slowly lengthen throughout adulthood.

title: You carry about as many bacteria as human cells.
explain: A 2016 estimate put it at roughly 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells.

title: Each eye has a blind spot.
explain: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no light receptors. Your brain fills in the gap.

title: A hiccup is your vocal cords snapping shut.
explain: Your diaphragm spasms, and the 'hic' is the sound of your vocal cords closing suddenly.

title: Yawning is contagious.
explain: Seeing, hearing or even reading about yawning can make you yawn.

title: One bone in your body isn't connected to any other bone.
explain: The hyoid bone in your throat is held in place only by muscles and ligaments.

title: You don't lose most heat through your head.
explain: Your head loses heat about as fast as any other uncovered part of your body.

title: Most people can tell apart around a million colors.
explain: Some estimates go even higher.

title: Your skeleton renews itself about every 10 years.
explain: Bone is constantly broken down and rebuilt throughout your life.

title: Your stomach growls even when you're not hungry.
explain: It's just gas and fluid moving through your gut. It's louder when your stomach is empty.

title: Your pupils widen when you think hard.
explain: They dilate with mental effort and interest, not just in darker light.

title: You make up to 1.5 liters of saliva a day.
explain: It helps you digest food and protects your teeth.

title: Fresh sweat has no smell.
explain: Body odor comes from bacteria breaking down sweat on your skin.

title: Your brain can't feel pain.
explain: Brain tissue has no pain receptors, which is why some brain surgery is done with patients awake.

title: Nerve signals can travel at over 400 km/h.
explain: The fastest nerve fibers carry signals at around 120 meters per second.

title: Your heart has its own electrical system.
explain: It generates its own beat, which is why a transplanted heart can keep beating without being connected to nerves.

title: Your appendix may not be useless.
explain: Scientists think it may store good gut bacteria to help restock your gut after illness.

title: Babies are born without bony kneecaps.
explain: Their kneecaps are made of cartilage and only turn to bone between the ages of about 3 and 5.

title: Earth isn't a perfect sphere.
explain: It bulges at the equator, so its equatorial diameter is about 43 km wider than from pole to pole.

title: Everest isn't the farthest point from Earth's center.
explain: Because of the equatorial bulge, Ecuador's Chimborazo peak sticks out farther into space.

title: Mauna Kea is taller than Everest.
explain: Measured from its base on the seafloor, the Hawaiian volcano is over 10,000 meters tall.

title: The Dead Sea shore is the lowest land on Earth.
explain: It sits about 430 meters below sea level and keeps getting lower as the sea shrinks.

title: The Pacific is bigger than all land combined.
explain: It covers about a third of Earth's surface.

title: Antarctica is the world's largest desert.
explain: A desert is defined by low rainfall, not heat, and Antarctica gets very little.

title: Days are getting longer.
explain: Tides slow Earth's rotation, adding about 2 milliseconds to the day every century.

title: Lightning strikes Earth about 44 times a second.
explain: That's roughly 1.4 billion flashes a year.

title: About half of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean.
explain: Tiny ocean plankton produce it through photosynthesis.

title: The Sahara used to be green.
explain: Between about 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, it had lakes, grasslands and hippos.

title: Earth's magnetic poles swap places.
explain: North and south have flipped many times. The last full reversal was about 780,000 years ago.

title: The magnetic north pole is moving.
explain: It has been drifting from Canada toward Siberia, at times by around 50 km a year.

title: There's more water in the air than in all rivers.
explain: At any moment, the atmosphere holds several times more water than every river on Earth.

title: You can swim between two continents in Iceland.
explain: The Silfra fissure lies between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates.

title: The Atlantic Ocean gets wider every year.
explain: The plates on either side move apart about 2.5 cm a year, roughly as fast as nails grow.

title: Everest is still growing.
explain: The collision of India and Asia pushes it up by a few millimeters a year.

title: Antarctica holds most of the world's fresh water.
explain: Its ice sheet contains about 70% of Earth's fresh water.

title: Everest would disappear in the Mariana Trench.
explain: The Challenger Deep is about 10,900 meters deep, over 2 km more than Everest is tall.

title: Earth has 4.4-billion-year-old crystals.
explain: Tiny zircon crystals from Western Australia are the oldest known pieces of Earth.

title: The biggest waterfall is underwater.
explain: The Denmark Strait cataract drops about 3.5 km beneath the ocean between Greenland and Iceland.

title: No bridge crosses the Amazon.
explain: Along its main stretch, the river has no bridges. Ferries do the job.

title: Lake Baikal holds about 20% of Earth's unfrozen surface fresh water.
explain: It's the deepest lake in the world at over 1,600 meters.

title: Earth is closest to the Sun in January.
explain: Seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun.

title: The Great Barrier Reef is visible from orbit.
explain: It's the largest structure made by living things.

title: Volcanoes can make their own lightning.
explain: Colliding ash particles in an eruption build up electric charge.

title: Some rocks float.
explain: Pumice is so full of gas bubbles that it floats on water.

title: Some sand dunes sing.
explain: Avalanching sand on certain dunes makes a low booming hum that can last minutes.

title: Earth's crust is thinner than an apple skin, in scale.
explain: Relative to Earth's size, the rocky crust is extremely thin.

title: The hottest air temperature ever recorded was 56.7°C.
explain: It was measured in Death Valley, California, in 1913.

title: The coldest recorded temperature was −89.2°C.
explain: It was measured at Vostok Station in Antarctica in 1983.

title: At the equator, you're spinning at about 1,670 km/h.
explain: You don't feel it because everything around you moves too.

title: Around 500,000 earthquakes are detected each year.
explain: About 100,000 are strong enough to be felt.

title: The 2011 Japan earthquake shortened the day.
explain: It shifted Earth's mass enough to make days about 1.8 microseconds shorter.

title: Most volcanic activity is underwater.
explain: The majority of Earth's eruptions happen along ocean ridges, unseen.

title: Most of the seafloor hasn't been mapped in detail.
explain: We have better maps of the surface of Mars than of much of our own ocean floor.

title: The Pacific is higher than the Atlantic at Panama.
explain: Sea level on the Pacific side is about 20 cm higher.

title: Hawaii is moving toward Japan.
explain: The Pacific plate carries it northwest by several centimeters a year.

title: A lake in Cameroon once exploded.
explain: In 1986, Lake Nyos released a huge cloud of carbon dioxide that killed about 1,700 people.

title: Icicles can form underwater.
explain: Brinicles grow down from sea ice and freeze anything they touch on the seafloor.

title: The Moon pulls on the ground too.
explain: The solid ground rises and falls with the tides by up to tens of centimeters.

title: Rainbows are actually full circles.
explain: From the ground, the horizon hides the bottom half. From a plane, you can sometimes see the whole ring.

title: The oceans hold about 97% of Earth's water.
explain: Most of the rest is frozen in ice caps and glaciers.

title: Dust from the Sahara fertilizes the Amazon.
explain: Winds carry mineral-rich dust across the Atlantic to the rainforest.

title: Earth gains tonnes of space dust every year.
explain: Thousands of tonnes of tiny particles from space fall on Earth every year.

title: The top of Everest was once under the sea.
explain: Its summit rock is marine limestone containing fossils of sea creatures.

title: There are hundreds of lakes under Antarctica.
explain: Liquid water lies beneath the ice, including Lake Vostok, buried under nearly 4 km of ice.

title: The sea is salty because of rocks.
explain: Rain slowly dissolves minerals from rocks, and rivers carry them to the ocean.

title: Russia spans 11 time zones.
explain: When it's morning in the west, it's already evening on the Pacific coast.

title: The word 'run' has over 600 meanings.
explain: It has one of the largest entries in the Oxford English Dictionary.

title: The dot on an 'i' has a name.
explain: It's called a tittle.

title: 'Goodbye' comes from 'God be with ye'.
explain: Over time, the phrase was shortened and blended into one word.

title: 'Rhythms' has no standard vowels.
explain: It's one of the longest English words without a, e, i, o or u.

title: 'Nice' used to mean foolish.
explain: It comes from Latin 'nescius', meaning ignorant, and took centuries to become a compliment.

title: Most languages call a pineapple 'ananas'.
explain: English is one of the few that doesn't.

title: An island in Spain has a whistled language.
explain: On La Gomera, Silbo Gomero turns Spanish into whistles that carry for kilometers.

title: Papua New Guinea has over 800 languages.
explain: It's the most linguistically diverse country on Earth.

title: Many languages are disappearing.
explain: Linguists estimate a large share of the world's 7,000 languages could vanish this century.

title: 'Alphabet' comes from its first two letters.
explain: Alpha and beta, the first letters of the Greek alphabet.

title: 'Ampersand' comes from a schoolroom chant.
explain: Children recited '& per se and' at the end of the alphabet, which blurred into one word.

title: English has no official regulator.
explain: Unlike French or Spanish, no official academy decides what's correct.

title: Some languages don't use left and right.
explain: Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr in Australia use north, south, east and west instead.

title: 'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo' is a real sentence.
explain: It uses buffalo as a city, an animal and a verb meaning to bully.

title: 'Salary' is linked to salt.
explain: It comes from Latin 'salarium'. The story that soldiers were paid in salt is probably a myth.

title: 'Muscle' means 'little mouse'.
explain: It comes from Latin 'musculus', perhaps because a flexing muscle looks like a mouse moving under skin.

title: 'Clue' comes from a ball of thread.
explain: A 'clew' was yarn, like the thread Theseus used to find his way out of the labyrinth.

title: Hawaiian has only 13 letters.
explain: Five vowels, seven consonants and a glottal stop called the ʻokina.

title: One language has just 12 letters.
explain: Rotokas, spoken in Papua New Guinea, has one of the smallest alphabets in the world.

title: Khmer has the longest alphabet.
explain: The Cambodian script has 74 letters.

title: 'OK' started as a joke.
explain: It came from 'oll korrect', a deliberate misspelling in an 1839 Boston newspaper.

title: Japanese uses three writing systems.
explain: Kanji, hiragana and katakana are often mixed within a single sentence.

title: 'Emoji' has nothing to do with 'emotion'.
explain: It's Japanese: 'e' means picture and 'moji' means character.

title: Shakespeare is the first recorded source of many words.
explain: Words like 'lonely' and 'eyeball' first appear in writing in his works.

title: A Welsh village has a 58-letter name.
explain: Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch is often shortened to Llanfair PG.

title: J was one of the last letters added to the alphabet.
explain: For centuries, I and J were treated as the same letter.

title: 'Gaslighting' comes from a play.
explain: The 1938 play Gas Light is about a husband who manipulates his wife into doubting reality.

title: 'Robot' comes from Czech.
explain: It comes from 'robota', meaning forced labor, first used in a 1920 play.

title: 'Quarantine' means forty days.
explain: It comes from Italian 'quaranta giorni', the time ships waited in Venice during plague outbreaks.

title: 'Disaster' means 'bad star'.
explain: It comes from Italian, reflecting an old belief that the stars controlled fate.

title: In Mandarin, 'ma' can mean mother or horse.
explain: It depends on the tone. Mandarin has four main tones, plus a neutral one.

title: 'Uncopyrightable' doesn't repeat any letter.
explain: It's one of the longest English words where every letter is different.

title: 'Huh?' exists in almost every language.
explain: A 2013 study found a word like 'huh' in all of the 31 languages it examined.

title: Esperanto has native speakers.
explain: It was invented in 1887, and some children grow up speaking it at home.

title: Hamlet has been translated into Klingon.
explain: The fictional Star Trek language has a full grammar and dictionary.

title: Sign languages aren't universal.
explain: American Sign Language is closer to French Sign Language than to British Sign Language.

title: 'Hello' became popular because of the telephone.
explain: Thomas Edison pushed it as the standard way to answer the phone.

title: 'Checkmate' comes from Persian.
explain: 'Shāh māt' roughly means 'the king is helpless'.

title: 'Jumbo' was an elephant.
explain: A famous circus elephant named Jumbo made the word mean 'huge'.

title: John Milton invented 'pandemonium'.
explain: In Paradise Lost, it's the capital of hell, meaning 'all demons'.

title: 'Nerd' first appeared in a Dr. Seuss book.
explain: It showed up in If I Ran the Zoo in 1950 as the name of a creature.

title: 'Serendipity' was coined in 1754.
explain: Horace Walpole made it up after a fairy tale called The Three Princes of Serendip.

title: Many languages don't separate blue and green.
explain: They use one word for both, and linguists call the combined color 'grue'.

title: Russian has two words for blue.
explain: 'Goluboy' is light blue and 'siniy' is dark blue, treated as different colors.

title: German can build extremely long words.
explain: Donaudampfschifffahrtsgesellschaftskapitän means 'Danube steamship company captain'.

title: Japanese has a word for unread books.
explain: 'Tsundoku' means buying books and letting them pile up without reading them.

title: The word for 'mother' often starts with M.
explain: From 'mama' to 'mère' to 'mā', it may be because 'm' is one of the first sounds babies make.

title: You can type 'typewriter' on one row.
explain: All its letters are on the top row of a QWERTY keyboard.

title: 'Bookkeeper' has three double letters in a row.
explain: oo, kk and ee, one after another.

title: Some languages have no fixed words for numbers.
explain: The Pirahã language in the Amazon reportedly uses words closer to 'few' and 'many'.

title: The first computer bug was a real bug.
explain: In 1947, engineers found a moth stuck in the Harvard Mark II computer and taped it into their logbook.

title: The first webcam watched a coffee pot.
explain: Cambridge researchers set it up in 1991 so they could see if the pot was empty.

title: QWERTY was designed for typewriters.
explain: The layout came from 1870s typewriters. Whether it was meant to slow typists down is debated.

title: An early 1 GB hard drive weighed around 250 kg.
explain: IBM's 3380 from 1980 was the size of a fridge and cost tens of thousands of dollars.

title: Apollo 11's computer had about 4 KB of RAM.
explain: It guided astronauts to the Moon with less memory than a simple modern calculator.

title: The first text message said 'Merry Christmas'.
explain: It was sent from a computer to a phone in 1992.

title: The first .com domain was registered in 1985.
explain: It was symbolics.com, and it's still around.

title: Email is older than the web.
explain: Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email in 1971, about 20 years before the web.

title: The first YouTube video is about elephants.
explain: 'Me at the zoo' was uploaded in 2005 by a co-founder and is only 19 seconds long.

title: CAPTCHA is an acronym.
explain: It stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart.

title: Wi-Fi doesn't stand for anything.
explain: The name was chosen by a branding firm because it sounded catchy.

title: Bluetooth is named after a Viking king.
explain: Harald Bluetooth united Danish tribes, and the logo combines his runic initials.

title: The Firefox logo isn't a fox.
explain: The animal is a red panda, which is sometimes called a firefox.

title: The first computer mouse was made of wood.
explain: Douglas Engelbart's 1964 prototype had a wooden shell and two metal wheels.

title: The first photo on the web was a band.
explain: In 1992, a CERN scientist uploaded a picture of a comedy band called Les Horribles Cernettes.

title: Space Invaders sped up by accident.
explain: The aliens moved faster as they were destroyed because the hardware had fewer to draw.

title: Most internet traffic crosses the ocean through cables.
explain: Undersea cables carry almost all data between continents, not satellites.

title: Sharks have bitten undersea cables.
explain: Cable companies have added protective layers partly because of it.

title: The first iPhone had no App Store.
explain: It came a year later, in 2008.

title: Spam email is named after a comedy sketch.
explain: In a Monty Python sketch, a group repeats 'Spam' until nothing else can be heard.

title: The word 'bit' was coined in 1947.
explain: Statistician John Tukey shortened 'binary digit'.

title: The first computer program was written in the 1840s.
explain: Ada Lovelace wrote an algorithm for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, which was never finished.

title: The first hard drive stored about 3.75 MB.
explain: IBM's 1956 RAMAC used 50 platters, each about 60 cm wide.

title: JavaScript was created in 10 days.
explain: Brendan Eich wrote the first version in May 1995.

title: Python is named after Monty Python.
explain: Its creator, Guido van Rossum, was a fan of the comedy group.

title: Many computers have a 2038 problem.
explain: Systems storing time as a 32-bit number will overflow on January 19, 2038.

title: Google comes from a misspelled number.
explain: A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros.

title: Amazon was almost called Cadabra.
explain: Jeff Bezos changed it after someone misheard it as 'cadaver'.

title: The first website is still online.
explain: CERN restored it at info.cern.ch.

title: GPS has to correct for Einstein's relativity.
explain: Satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast compared with clocks on the ground.

title: The save icon is a floppy disk.
explain: Many people using it today have never seen a real floppy disk.

title: The Apple I sold for $666.66.
explain: Steve Wozniak liked repeating digits, not the number's meaning.

title: The first mobile phone call was a brag.
explain: In 1973, Motorola's Martin Cooper called a rival at Bell Labs from a New York street.

title: ENIAC weighed about 27 tonnes.
explain: The 1945 computer used around 17,500 vacuum tubes and filled a large room.

title: SOS doesn't stand for anything.
explain: It was chosen because three dots, three dashes and three dots are easy to send and recognize.

title: One of the first video games was tennis.
explain: Tennis for Two ran on an oscilloscope in 1958.

title: Pac-Man was inspired by a pizza.
explain: Designer Toru Iwatani says a pizza with a missing slice gave him the idea.

title: The bumps on F and J have a purpose.
explain: They help you find the home row without looking.

title: The hashtag was proposed in a tweet.
explain: Chris Messina suggested using # to group topics in 2007.

title: The first tweet was 'just setting up my twttr'.
explain: Jack Dorsey posted it in March 2006.

title: The first emoji set had 176 icons.
explain: Shigetaka Kurita designed them in 1999 for a Japanese phone service.

title: An early PC virus included its authors' address.
explain: The Brain virus from 1986 was written by two brothers in Pakistan, who included their contact details.

title: A Kodak engineer invented the digital camera.
explain: Steven Sasson's 1975 prototype took 23 seconds to record one 0.01-megapixel image.

title: Velcro was inspired by burrs.
explain: George de Mestral studied the burrs stuck to his dog's fur after a walk.

title: QR codes were invented for car parts.
explain: A Japanese company created them in 1994 to track parts in factories.

title: The first barcode scan was a pack of gum.
explain: In 1974, a pack of Wrigley's gum was scanned in an Ohio supermarket.

title: Programmers debug by talking to rubber ducks.
explain: Explaining code line by line to a toy duck often reveals the bug.

title: Hard drive heads fly just nanometers above the disk.
explain: The gap is far smaller than a speck of dust.
